endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Keeping materials current may not require a heavy lift if a lightweight review process is built into existing deployment and update workflows.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether reviewing patient AI transparency materials at each new deployment or material update keeps those materials accurate, and no study was supplied that documents how often such materials become outdated. The recommendation currently rests on one governance framework, the CHAI playbooks, which frames the practice as optional ("may") and low-burden.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned beyond no direct evidence. The single endorsement comes from a framework and uses permissive language. Expert consensus of this kind indicates plausibility, but it does not estimate effect on accuracy of materials or on patient understanding.

The CHAI playbooks state that keeping materials current may not require a heavy lift if a lightweight review step is added to existing deployment and update workflows. That statement is an expectation. No supplied study measures staff time, cost, or completion rates for such a review step, so feasibility at scale remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that first measure how often patient-facing AI information diverges from deployed system behavior after launches and updates, and then compare accuracy, staff time, and patient comprehension between systems that embed a review step in deployment workflows and systems that do not.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether review processes keep translated and plain-language versions current at the same rate as English materials is unknown, and systems serving these patients have no data to guide them.
